canonicalExplanation.summary: C++20 **ranges** make algorithms take whole containers (`std::ranges::sort(v)` instead of `v.begin(), v.end()`) and add **views**: lightweight, **lazy** adaptors you chain with `|`. `v | std::views::filter(is_even) | std::views::transform(square)` describes a pipeline; **nothing is computed until you iterate** it. Views **don't own** data: they **refer to** the underlying container. So the container must **stay alive and unchanged** (no push_back or erase) while you use the view. To keep results, **materialise** them into a new container.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner returns `v | std::views::filter(...)` from a function where v is a local vector. Iterating the returned view reads a destroyed vector. Separately, they push_back into the vector while a view over it is being iterated. A filter view over a live vector is iterated while the vector remains alive and structurally unchanged. In this lesson you'll build and explain a simple filtered and transformed range pipeline.

examples.title: Even squares from a live vector
examples.situation: A filter view over a live vector is iterated while the vector remains alive and structurally unchanged.
walkthrough: **A filter view over a live vector:** nums | views::filter(even) | views::transform(square).
**Is iterated while the vector remains alive:** the loop runs inside main, where nums lives.
**And structurally unchanged:** no push_back until the loop ends; the output will be 4 16 36.
examples.result: The pipeline computes exactly the needed values without dangling or invalidation.

examples.title: The dangling returned view
examples.situation: get_evens() returns a view over its local vector. The caller prints garbage.
walkthrough: The view referred to a vector destroyed on return.
Return std::vector<int> built from the view (materialise).
Or let the caller own the vector and pass it by reference.
examples.result: The caller receives data it owns.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Every range view owns a copied collection, so it remains valid after the original container is destroyed.
misconceptions.correction: Views over containers refer to the original elements and don't own them. They dangle when the container is destroyed and misbehave when it's modified structurally.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The dangling returned view", what did the view refer to?

analogy.example: A view is like **a set of instructions for reading a book**: "only even pages, and read each aloud twice". The instructions don't contain the book. If the book is taken away (destroyed) or pages are inserted mid-reading (push_back), the instructions stop making sense. To keep the result, **write it down** (materialise).
usefulFor: write it down to keep it
limitations: Reading instructions are free; so is creating a view.

steps.explanation: A filter view over a live vector only describes the work.

nearTransfer.prompt: Build a pipeline over a vector of words: keep words longer than 3 letters, transform to their lengths, take the first 3. Print it, then materialise to a vector<std::size_t>.

farTransfer.prompt: Rewrite a hand-written loop that filters, transforms and sums into a ranges pipeline plus std::ranges::fold_left or accumulate over the view. Write a test, then write a buggy version returning a view from a function, and fix it by returning a vector.
scaffold: fold_left is C++23; accumulate works on begin/end.

remediation.explanation: For every view ask: **who owns the data, is it still alive, and will anyone change its size while I iterate?** Materialise if the answer is uncertain.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The dangling returned view".

recap.summary: To build range pipelines, chain lazy views like filter and transform with |, use whole-range algorithms like std::ranges::sort, remember views compute on iteration and don't own their data, keep the source alive and structurally unchanged while iterating, and materialise results into containers to keep them.
